Ekaterina Matveeva is an entrepreneur, interdisciplinary researcher and international AI-and-education specialist working at the intersection of artificial intelligence, multilingualism, intercultural communication and human development. She is based in Argentina and brings practical AI industry experience together with research on language, culture and inclusive participation.

She is Founder and Director of Amolingua, an international education technology company specialising in language learning, cultural intelligence and multilingual soft skills. She also serves as Director at Lingo+, an EU-co-funded teacher-training initiative. Amolingua’s Language Institute operates through Texas State University Continuing Education.

Since 2023, Matveeva has led multilingual AI consulting and prompt-development teams for AI companies in Asia and collaborated with US-based AI companies on reinforcement learning from human feedback and model evaluation. She has coordinated international writer and reviewer teams and advised on linguistic relevance, conversational fluency, pedagogical quality, cultural representation and contextual alignment.

Her interdisciplinary research includes the Language Alter Ego framework and explores how multilingualism and intercultural environments shape personality, cognition, communication and identity. The work draws on autoethnographic research, 21 interviews across nine countries, observations of multilingual learning environments, and study of linguistic imperialism and sociocultural adaptation. She also co-organises the Year of AI Challenged roundtable series and edits the forthcoming book of the same name.

As the Coalition’s International Collaboration and Partnerships Lead, Matveeva works to connect researchers, academic institutions, technology practitioners, policy experts and youth-led organisations across regions. Her Founding Committee remit includes youth, multilingualism and culturally inclusive AI governance, with a focus on ensuring that linguistic and cultural diversity and Global South perspectives are represented in international research and policy dialogue.

For her first 90 days, she proposes a focused expert contribution to the preliminary UNESCO Recommendation on AI and Youth. The work would review the draft, identify gaps relating to multilingualism, cultural diversity, youth agency and equitable participation, and develop three to five evidence-based textual recommendations. She also proposes targeted input from researchers and youth stakeholders across regions, particularly the Global South, for consideration through appropriate UNESCO-related and Coalition channels.

Dr. Jelina Haines is an interdisciplinary researcher, policy professional and institutional leader working across AI governance, information ethics, Indigenous data sovereignty, research governance and culturally responsive policy. Her qualifications include a PhD in Computer Science and Indigenous Studies, a Master of Public Policy, and postgraduate training in information management, digital preservation, education and cultural management.

As SIG Cabinet Director for the Association for Information Science and Technology (ASIS&T), she provides strategic governance and oversight across 19 international Special Interest Groups. She previously chaired ASIS&T’s Information Ethics and Policy and Digital Libraries groups. She is also Co-Chair of the Catalyst Now Oceania Chapter and Founder of SunRay Wearable Art, connecting institutional leadership, community-led innovation and creative practice.

Her research is grounded in more than two decades of collaboration with Ngarrindjeri Elders and communities. She developed the Weave & Talk framework and a Meaningful Engagement approach, and has led community-based research involving sensitive cultural and health information. Her work emphasizes consent-aware, culturally safe practices for data collection, documentation and knowledge stewardship, and advances ethical and decolonial approaches to Indigenous knowledge governance.

As the Coalition’s International Research & Policy Lead, Dr. Haines aims to strengthen comparative research and international engagement on inclusive AI governance. Her work focuses on Indigenous data sovereignty, collective rights, community authority, institutional accountability and culturally responsive policy. This complements her Founding Committee remit on Indigenous Knowledge & Community Governance and her priority of moving beyond consultation toward meaningful participation and shared decision-making.

For her first 90 days, she proposes a comparative policy briefing and evidence map on Indigenous data sovereignty, community participation and collective rights across selected Global South and Indigenous contexts. The research would review governance strategies, laws and institutional practices; identify where affected communities can influence decisions about their data and knowledge; and document practical approaches and policy gaps. Proposed outputs include a 15–20-page publication-ready briefing, an executive summary, a comparative evidence map and a practical framework for assessing participation and accountability.

1. PROFESSIONAL PROFILE

Nafiul Ahmad Rafi is an AI governance and public policy researcher, policy architect, technology developer, and institutional founder based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. He is the Founding Director of Atlas AI Institute and Founder and Chairman of the Atlas Global South AI Policy Coalition.

His work focuses on developing practical AI governance frameworks, comparative policy research, institutional readiness systems, digital public infrastructure, and public-interest technology for Bangladesh and the wider Global South.

He works across the full chain of AI governance development: from comparative research and regulatory analysis to policy architecture, technical system development, and real-world public-interest applications.

A central component of his research is comparative AI policy analysis across more than 75 countries. His wider research portfolio includes a 38-country AI governance monograph, national governance assessments, comparative policy maturity research, and the development of AI governance intelligence infrastructure.

He founded Atlas AI Institute to address a structural gap in international AI governance: developing economies need more than imported policy templates. They need context-sensitive regulatory frameworks, institutional capacity, technical infrastructure, and the ability to independently assess and govern emerging technologies.

His technical work includes the development of AI governance monitoring and assessment systems, evidence-based policy intelligence platforms, civic technology, information verification systems, geographic information tools, and digital infrastructure.

His applied projects include NagorikBD, an AI-enabled civic technology platform with reported coverage across more than 190 upazilas in three divisions of Bangladesh, and FactCheckBD, an AI-based fact-checking and digital verification system built around a large verified information dataset.

His research and technical portfolio includes the Atlas AI Governance Observatory, Atlas AI Governance Intelligence Index, Atlas AI Policy Index, Global AI Policy Maturity Index, Atlas Global South AI Policy Framework, GhostCluster, Atlas Impact GIS, Atlas OS, and other research and development initiatives.

Previously, he worked as a researcher within the Adviser's Team at the ICT Division of the Government of Bangladesh from November 2024 to January 2026. His research work included cybersecurity legislation, personal data protection, and digital governance, including research relating to the Cyber Security Act 2025 and the Personal Data Protection Ordinance 2026.

His guiding principle is that research should lead to policy, policy should inform implementation, and technology should produce meaningful public impact.

---

2. FOUNDING LEADERSHIP

Founder & Chairman — Atlas Global South AI Policy Coalition

Nafiul Ahmad Rafi initiated the Atlas Global South AI Policy Coalition as an international research, policy, and institutional collaboration initiative under the founding institutional leadership of Atlas AI Institute.

The Coalition responds to the limited and fragmented participation of developing countries, Global South researchers, policymakers, and institutions in international AI governance.

It aims to connect researchers, academics, legal professionals, technology practitioners, civil society representatives, and institutional leaders across different countries and regions.

The initiative is designed to move beyond symbolic international membership and establish a practical collaborative platform where members can:

- Produce comparative AI governance research.
- Develop joint policy briefs and publications.
- Share national and regional policy experiences.
- Contribute to international AI governance discussions.
- Strengthen institutional and research partnerships.
- Develop locally grounded policy recommendations.
- Support capacity-building and knowledge exchange.
- Increase Global South participation in international AI governance.

As Founder and Chairman, Nafiul Ahmad Rafi provides the founding vision, strategic direction, and institutional leadership of the Coalition.

His objective is to build a credible international platform that converts the expertise of its membership into substantive research, practical policy contributions, and sustained cross-regional cooperation.

FOUNDING PHILOSOPHY

The future of AI governance should not be determined exclusively by the countries and institutions that possess the greatest technological and economic power.

Developing economies must have the capacity to shape their own AI governance priorities, strengthen regulatory institutions, protect their digital sovereignty, and participate meaningfully in international standard-setting.

The Coalition seeks to advance this objective through research, collaboration, institutional development, and policy engagement.

4. FLAGSHIP COMPARATIVE AI POLICY RESEARCH

GLOBAL AI POLICY REVIEW 2026

Comparative Research Across 75+ Countries

The Global AI Policy Review is a flagship comparative research publication examining AI policy and governance developments across more than 75 countries.

The research documents national policy approaches, regulatory developments, institutional arrangements, and governance priorities across different jurisdictions.

It provides a comparative resource for researchers, policymakers, public institutions, and organisations examining how AI governance is developing internationally.

Research dimensions include:

- National AI strategies and policy frameworks.
- AI regulatory approaches and institutional mandates.
- Responsible AI principles and ethical governance.
- Data protection and privacy.
- AI safety, risk management, and accountability.
- Public-sector AI adoption.
- Institutional readiness and governance capacity.
- Digital sovereignty and international cooperation.

The review is a comparative research publication. Its coverage does not imply operational presence in every country or constitute an official government assessment.

The analysis uses a SWOT-oriented approach to identify:

Neaz Mujeri is a researcher and AI governance and literacy professional working at the intersection of artificial intelligence, sustainability, systems thinking, and inclusive development. He is Executive Director & CEO of the Center for Research Initiatives (CRI), where he leads research and knowledge initiatives on AI literacy, responsible AI adoption, and sustainable development. His research interests include AI governance, Generative AI, AI literacy and capability-building, sustainability, and the role of AI in advancing the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly in the Global South.

Neaz has academic and research experience across Bangladesh, Canada, the United Arab Emirates, and Australia, including research on Generative AI and sustainability. He has authored and co-authored books and peer-reviewed research and actively contributes to professional and academic discussions on responsible AI and emerging AI governance frameworks. His work is guided by a strong commitment to ensuring that perspectives and priorities from the Global South are meaningfully represented in the development of global AI policy and governance.

I did my PhD from the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Rutgers University, New Jersey. My research works lie at the intersection of Signal Processing, Machine Learning and Wireless Communication. At present I'm focusing on developing machine learning algorithm for Device Free Indoor Localization using WiFi Signals. I have prior research experience in Speech Enhancement using Wavelet Packet Transform. Currently I am focusing my research on developing IoT based healthcare system in Bangladesh

I am looking for motivated and hard working students for Masters and PhD in BUET in the above mentioned area of machine learning, AI and IoT.

Zico Chakma is a Communication and Journalism graduate from the University of Chittagong, Bangladesh, and is currently pursuing his M.S.S. in Communication and Journalism at the same institution. He is a communication professional with a particular focus on Indigenous storytelling, documentary storytelling, and community-centered communication.

As a youth fellow at ICCAD, Zico is engaged in exploring emerging issues at the intersection of communication, technology, and society. His interests extend to the Indigenous and environmental dimensions of AI policy and governance, particularly how emerging technologies can be developed and governed in ways that are inclusive, ethical, and responsive to Indigenous communities and environmental concerns.

Through storytelling, research, and youth engagement, he aims to amplify underrepresented voices and contribute to more inclusive approaches to communication, technology, and policymaking.

I am an AI safety and governance (AIGP) researcher working at the intersection of technology, public interest, and global risks.

My professional background is rooted in infectious disease epidemiology, molecular biology and data science. Previously, I worked at the World Health Organization, where I delivered mission-critical analytics supporting outbreak response in multi-country deployments, enabling rapid institutional decision-making under uncertainty.  I led outbreak analytics during global health emergencies (eg. Go.Data software implementation for contact tracing for Ebola and COVID-19), and pandemic H1N1 influenza, Ebola, plague and COVID-19 outbreaks , across diverse contexts such as the Netherlands, the UK, Madagascar, Guinea, Mali, Laos PDR, Guatemala, the DRC, Fiji, and Moldova. This work required making high-stakes decisions under deep uncertainty, managing complex systems, and anticipating cascading failures, experiences that continue to shape how I approach AI risk.

As AI systems have become increasingly powerful and socially embedded, my focus has shifted toward AI safety, governance, and policy, particularly where failures could have large-scale or irreversible consequences. I work on issues including AI risk governance, algorithmic accountability and auditing, and the design of institutional and policy frameworks capable of responding to rapidly advancing technologies. I am currently working at the EU AI office on AI Safety. The European AI Office supports the development and adoption of trustworthy Artificial Intelligence (AI) solutions, while protecting people against risks.

Sithar Norbu is a Chief Program Officer with the Public Service Delivery Division, Prime Minister’s Office, Royal Government of Bhutan. His work focuses on simplifying and standardizing government services, improving citizen journeys, strengthening inter-agency coordination, and expanding integrated service channels for citizens and businesses.

He holds an International Master’s in Artificial Intelligence for Public Services from Universidad Politécnica de Madrid and a Bachelor of Science (Honours) in Computer Science from the University of Delhi. His professional interests include citizen-centred digital government, GovTech, service design, digital inclusion, responsible AI and data governance.

I hold an MSc in Digital Society at the University of Edinburgh under the Chevening Award, a postgraduate degree in Business Administration from FGV, and a degree in International Relations. I currently work as a Project Management Consultant for the UK Government’s Digital Access Programme (DAP), supporting the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO). In this role, I manage projects focused on digital technologies, artificial intelligence, digital policy, digital safety, and meaningful connectivity.

Throughout my career, I have worked with several international organisations and leading institutions, including the University of Cambridge, Microsoft, The Ohio State University, and Facebook (now Meta). At Meta, I served as a Programme Manager.

At Microsoft, I also served as the leader of BAM in Brazil, and Business Manager for the External and Corporate Affairs department connecting digital technology and policy. At Microsft I developed strategies and initiatives aimed at creating a more diverse and inclusive environment within the technology sector. My work focused on professional development, self-awareness, networking, and advancing discussions on racial equity in Brazil. I also created initiatives to raise awareness of digital exclusion in Brazil.

As a consultant to the British Government’s Digital Access Programme, I have managed several projects focused on the intersection of technology, public policy, and social impact. One example is the “Digital Technologies and Environmental Sustainability in Brazil” project, which focused on mapping and disseminating research on the use of artificial intelligence to support environmental sustainability while addressing and mitigating the risks associated with its adoption. 

Another example is a Digital Citizenship project implemented in collaboration with SaferNet and Brazil’s Ministry of Education. I played an instrumental role in designing and implementing digital safety and citizenship courses that reached 145,548 students across 1,065 schools in all 27 Brazilian states. I co-wrote the project proposal, managed its implementation, and ensured alignment with both Brazilian and UK Government priorities. By supporting the integration of digital safety initiatives into public policy, I contributed to significant nationwide impact, demonstrating my ability to manage large-scale projects and navigate complex international collaborations.

International Relations undergraduate student at the Federal University of Goiás (UFG) and Researcher at the Center of Excellence in Artificial Intelligence (CEIA)—Latin America's largest AI research center—where she develops the "CEIA AI Policy & Governance Lab" project, investigating digital sovereignty, international security, and global AI governance. First winner of the 1st Mônica de Menezes Campos Award by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Brazil and Project Leader for the Government of the State of Goiás, she works strategically at the intersection of technology, foreign policy, and innovation.

I am a Brazilian social impact and innovation professional with more than 25 years of experience working at the intersection of socio-environmental development, inclusion, institutional transformation and, increasingly, artificial intelligence, in Brazil and in some African countries.
I am the co-founder of SUL – Inteligência para Impacto, a Brazil-based impact tech focused on developing and applying AI to social and environmental challenges in the Global South. My work combines AI literacy, responsible AI adoption, knowledge development and the design of AI solutions for organizations and communities working in contexts of social and economic inequality.
Through SUL, I co-lead the development of Mariah, an AI-based educational and business support platform designed to expand access to knowledge, capabilities and decision support for nano and microentrepreneurs, particularly those underserved by conventional technology and business support systems. Mariah combines education, conversational AI and practical business support to make technology more accessible and useful in everyday economic life.
We are also developing the AI Brain for Impact, a knowledge infrastructure designed to organize and connect curated knowledge, support knowledge management and enable collaborative knowledge creation across the social impact ecosystem. The goal is not simply to make information searchable, but to create an intelligent layer through which people and organizations can access, connect, interpret and collectively develop knowledge for action.
My work is grounded in the belief that responsible AI in the Global South must go beyond principles and regulation to address questions of access, agency, capacity, inclusion and real-world impact. I hold a Master's degree in International Relations and Development Studies and MBAs in Entrepreneurship & Business Management and Human Resources Development.

I am an AI governance and information security professional and a PhD candidate in Business Administration at UNIVALI, Brazil. My work bridges research and practice, focusing on responsible AI governance, trustworthy AI, human agency, and the societal impacts of generative AI. I was a Visiting PhD Scholar at Bentley University, where I conducted research at the intersection of AI, strategy, governance, and society. I currently work on translating AI governance principles and international frameworks into organizational practices in Brazil.

Ph.D. Candidate in Sustainability Education at Prescott College, NSF Research Fellow, and accredited Independent International Expert (OMEI Geneva N°2688). Expert Contributor to the ITU-T Focus Group on AI for Smart Cities (FG-AI4SSC) and Africa AI Policy Fellow. Co-author of the Africa AI Governance Index 2026, specializing in AI-enabled resilience of critical infrastructure, cybersecurity governance, and digital sustainability across the Global South.

Soumana Dama is a software engineer and AI practitioner from Burkina Faso, currently pursuing a Master’s degree in Emerging Networks, IoT and Embedded Intelligence at Université Joseph Ki-Zerbo. His work spans artificial intelligence, machine learning, NLP, multilingual AI for low-resource African languages, computer vision, and agentic AI systems.

He is the Founder & Lead AI Engineer of Scoinvestigator AI, a multi-agent scientific research assistant designed to help researchers explore scientific literature, synthesize evidence, and reason across complex information. He has also developed AI technologies for Mooré and Dioula and applied AI solutions in areas including agriculture and sustainable development.

Through building and deploying AI systems, he has developed a strong interest in AI governance, responsible AI, AI reliability, and the challenges of developing and deploying AI in low-resource contexts. He is particularly interested in ensuring that AI governance reflects the realities, priorities, and technological needs of the Global South.

Douglas Mbang Massom is an international research professional and public-interest AI governance specialist working across artificial intelligence, digital health, humanitarian technology and responsible innovation in low- and middle-income countries. He is Research Manager at Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), Founder and Research Director of Civic Oversight and Management for Public-Interest AI Systems (COMPASS), and a Fellow of the Africa Strategic Policy and AI Resource Centre (AFRI-SPARC).

His multi-country research has examined the testing, adoption and deployment of machine-learning tools in healthcare across resource-constrained settings. He contributed to a six-country evaluation of decentralised childhood tuberculosis diagnosis that brought together clinicians, economists, modellers and national programmes and generated policy recommendations for the World Health Organization. His collaborative work spans teams across Africa, Asia and Europe and includes studies on digital health implementation in Burkina Faso.

Massom’s AI governance research focuses on public-interest oversight, ethical deployment and institutional capacity in real-world healthcare and humanitarian settings. His work includes a reflective assessment of an NGO-supported AI cervical-cancer screening programme in Malawi against WHO ethical principles and a proposed minimum ethical floor for AI in humanitarian action. He also studies the operational realities of digital diagnostics and electronic health registers in low-resource environments.

As the Coalition’s International Research Collaboration & Partnerships Lead, he aims to connect research institutions, humanitarian organisations, civil society, public-health practitioners and AI policy communities. His Founding Committee remit is Research Collaboration & Partnerships, with an emphasis on equitable partnerships, shared agenda-setting, co-authorship, fair attribution and Global South research leadership rather than extractive collaboration.

For his first 90 days, he proposes a Global South AI Governance Partnership Map and Engagement Framework. The plan is to map at least 25 institutions working on AI governance in healthcare and humanitarian settings, engage 10 priority partners, and target at least three commitments through letters of intent or agreed joint work. The framework would set expectations for shared priorities, co-authorship, data governance and attribution, and culminate in a report identifying collaborative research, policy briefs and events for the Coalition.

I am a computer scientist and AI researcher from Cameroon. My work sits at the intersection of artificial intelligence, language, and the realities of communities that are often poorly represented in technology.

I became interested in these questions through research rather than policy. Working on multilingual NLP and AI safety, I have seen how an AI system can behave differently depending on the language, cultural context, and people represented in a prompt. That experience pushed me beyond the question of whether an AI system works, toward a harder question: **works for whom, and according to whose assumptions?**

My research has included building multilingual datasets and studying how large language models respond to culturally grounded information. I am particularly interested in what these findings mean for AI governance in Africa, where policy is often developing alongside technologies that were not designed with African languages, institutions, or social realities in mind.

I want my work to help ensure that Africa is not simply a market, testing ground, or case study for AI, but a place where ideas about how AI should be built and governed are also being developed.

I am an Ecuadorian lawyer working at the intersection of public law and the governance of automated decision-making inside public institutions. Gábor Soós, PhD, is an international governance specialist, researcher and coalition-builder with 25 years of experience in multilateral cooperation, cultural and knowledge diplomacy, education, institutional coordination and sustainable development. He is a Visiting Research Fellow at the United Nations University Institute on Comparative Regional Integration Studies (UNU-CRIS). From 2016 to 2026, he served as Secretary-General of the Hungarian National Commission for UNESCO, following earlier diplomatic service as Deputy Permanent Delegate of Hungary to UNESCO and Alternate Member of UNESCO’s Executive Board.

His work includes international negotiations, multilateral policy development, cultural heritage governance and institutional coordination. He contributed to the drafting of UNESCO’s 2003 Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage and later served as Rapporteur of its Intergovernmental Committee.

His current research explores AI governance through human agency, cultural and cognitive sovereignty, education and community participation. He initiated the World-Shaped AI Coalition (WOSAIC), an international network connecting researchers, educators, communities and institutions across Africa, Asia, Europe and the Caribbean. He also initiated Source2Sea – Bartók 3.0 Connectivity, a UN Ocean Decade project linking ecological knowledge, cultural heritage, education and emerging technologies through locally grounded work.

As Chair and Strategic Coordination Lead of the Coalition, Soós proposes a shared leadership model that includes a woman Co-Chair from the Global South. His priorities connect AI and youth rights, education, cross-sector governance, institutional partnerships and community-grounded research, with an emphasis on Global South representation and reciprocal collaboration.

For his first 90 days, he proposes coordinating an inaugural Coalition Policy Brief on AI, Youth and Human Agency to inform emerging international work on young people’s rights and well-being in the digital age. The proposed process includes at least three regional consultations with youth, educators, researchers and civil society across Global South regions, leading to an 8–10-page public brief with five to seven actionable recommendations. Topics include cognitive and narrative sovereignty, youth participation, culturally grounded AI education, human agency and well-being. The work would also establish a repeatable consultation-to-policy method for the Coalition.

My work focuses on AI-enabled newsroom workflows, misinformation and deepfake detection, digital verification systems, and editorial strategy at scale. I have led and strengthened high-impact fact-checking operations, countering coordinated disinformation campaigns and viral misinformation through investigative rigor and technology-led solutions.

I have participated in 70+ national and international engagements as a speaker, expert, or delegate, representing Indian journalism at global media forums, academic institutions, and policy discussions. My professional and academic associations include the London School of Economics (LSE), University of Oxford, Columbia Journalism School, East-West Center, and global media integrity networks such as the International Fact-Checking Network (IFCN) and Google News Initiative (GNI).

Recipient of multiple professional awards and holder of international certifications in fact-checking, digital verification, and AI-media practices. Known for translating complex technologies into practical, ethical, and newsroom-ready solutions that strengthen journalistic integrity in the digital age.

Radhika Venkataraman is a Staff UX Researcher working on AI trust and safety, based in Bengaluru. She brings 25 years of qualitative research across consumer insights, ethnography and UX, and teaches qualitative methods and cultural strategy at MICA. Her current research looks at how AI systems handle non-Western English, using Indian English as the primary case, and at where cultural bias enters the evaluation and tooling layer rather than the model itself. She is a part-time PhD candidate and mentors early-career researchers through WIRE and upGrad. She also writes essays and criticism at primalsoup.in, with work published in the New York Times, Out of Print and Punch.

I am an independent legal and policy researcher from India working at the intersection of artificial intelligence governance, human rights, international law, and responsible technology. My research interests include AI accountability, human oversight, digital rights, emerging technologies, and the governance implications of AI in high-stakes contexts. I hold a BA.LLB (Hons.) and have undertaken international training in human rights, international humanitarian law, AI governance, intellectual property, and sustainable development. I am particularly interested in bringing legal and Global South perspectives to evidence-based AI governance research and policy.
I am interested in medtech using AI

Rushikesh Kokare is a youth professional and researcher working at the intersection of public policy, education, international affairs, technology, and youth leadership. He holds a Postgraduate Diploma in Liberal Studies as a Young India Fellow at Ashoka University, with an interdisciplinary academic foundation in governance, international relations, public policy, and contemporary global affairs. He currently works as a Consultant with Teach For India and SCERT and is a Youth IGF India Research Fellow, working on issues including digital rights, AI governance, cybersecurity, data protection, and the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) framework.

He has engaged with international and youth-focused platforms, including the World Bank Group Youth Summit as a delegate, UNICEF YuWaah Youth Advisory Board Member, the Better Future Forum, and BRICS-related engagements. He has also delivered a TED-style talk at Ashoka University. These experiences have strengthened his capabilities in policy research, international dialogue, communication, stakeholder engagement, and cross-cultural collaboration.

His interests span AI governance, digital rights, education, emerging technologies, technology and security, and public policy, with a particular interest in how technology can advance equitable access to education and opportunities. He is especially interested in ensuring that technology governance is inclusive, rights-respecting, evidence-based, and responsive to the realities and priorities of communities across the Global South.

I am an Assistant Professor in the Information Systems area at TAPMI Bengaluru, Manipal Academy of Higher Education. I teaches AI for Managers to undergraduate and MBA students. My research interests include the impact of AI on the workforce, education, and public policy, with a particular focus on AI-enabled learning and online grievance redressal systems, including Voice AI and hybrid human–chatbot models.

Major Vineet Kumar is a globally recognized leader in cyber diplomacy and cyber peacebuilding who has redefined cybersecurity as a force for social good. As Founder and Global President of CyberPeace, he has spent nearly three decades building one of the world’s largest citizen driven movements for online safety, inclusion, and digital resilience, impacting more than 200 million people across 112 countries.

An alumnus of Cranfield University, GCSP Geneva, and the University of Cambridge, Vineet is a Chevening Fellow of the UK Government and an alumnus of the U.S. Department of State’s International Visitor Leadership Program. He has also participated in the British Council Future Leaders Programme 2017. He is associated with prestigious academic institutions as an Adjunct Faculty Member and Professor of Practice. As a subject matter expert, he has contributed to United Nations, government, and parliamentary committees, consultations, and expert commentaries on cybersecurity, AI safety, cyber policy, and digital trust.

He leads global collaborations with the United Nations, G20, Commonwealth Secretariat, ITU, ICANN, leading technology platforms, and other international institutions, helping shape global norms on AI safety, cybersecurity, and digital trust. He has trained diplomats and senior government officials from more than 100 countries, authored multiple acclaimed books, published several IEEE papers, and holds multiple patents in cybersecurity and AI safety.

A recipient of 13 international and 25 national awards, Vineet’s recognitions include Entrepreneur Magazine’s Social Entrepreneur of the Year 2025, The Times of India Social Entrepreneur of the Year 2025, and the National Youth Award 2014 to 2015, the Government of India’s highest youth honour. He was also recognized as a Finalist for the World Economic Forum Social Entrepreneur of the Year Award in 2021, nominated as a Young Global Leader Class of 2026, and named a Semi Finalist for Forbes 30 Under 30 Asia in 2018.

He embodies the mission of using technology to empower people, strengthen peace, and build a trusted digital future for humanity. He has been a distinguished speaker at leading global forums, including the United Nations General Assembly, UN Security Council Counter Terrorism Committee, UN Internet Governance Forum, ITU WSIS Forum, Global Cybersecurity Forum, UN Cybercrime Convention negotiations, SPIEF 2025, the Responsible AI in the Military Summit in South Korea, and the Valdai Discussion Club Annual Forum.

His work and thought leadership have been featured by leading international and national media outlets, including Forbes, TIME, BBC, CNN, Channel 4, TechCrunch, Mashable, Radio France Internationale, India Today, Times Now, NDTV, ANI, and Rajya Sabha TV.

Anis Fuad is a researcher and lecturer in public health informatics and digital health at Universitas Gadjah Mada, Indonesia. With more than 15 years of experience, he has worked with government agencies, international organizations, healthcare providers, and professional associations on digital health policy, health information systems, interoperability, data governance, regulatory innovation, and responsible AI in health. He serves on the Governing Council of the Asia eHealth Information Network and leads the Data and Information division of the Indonesian Hospital Association. Trained in medicine and medical informatics, he has authored more than 40 international scientific publications. His current interests include responsible AI governance, AI-enabled public health surveillance, digital health regulation, and strengthening institutional capacity for equitable digital transformation in low- and middle-income countries.

In summary, I have experience with relevant interventions in a wide range of leadership in thematic issues, ranging from developing and financing tech startups, environmental science, renewable energy, and climate finance to democratic governance.

Faisal has a BCSE (Hons) from Latrobe University, an MSc from the London School of Economics and Political Science, and a PhD from Universitas Indonesia.

Specialities: tech startup, blockchain technology, cryptocurrencies, fintech, climate change policy, infrastructure development, democratic governance, sales and marketing, CDM, renewable energy, carbon finance, REDD+, trust fund, ICT for Development, ASEAN Region. Project Management, Programme Planning and Management, Monitoring and Evaluation, Advisory Services

Faisal is a recreational endurance athlete who competed in several Ironman 70.3 distances.

Farhan Helmy is Founder and CEO of ASCODI Lab, working at the intersection of systems thinking, AI, geospatial intelligence, climate and sustainability, and inclusive development. With more than three decades of experience in environmental and climate policy, geospatial analysis, systems approaches, and multi-stakeholder governance, his work increasingly focuses on how AI and emerging computational technologies can strengthen public decision-making while remaining accountable to communities. He previously contributed to Indonesia’s climate-policy processes, including engagement in UNFCCC negotiations. His current work explores community-centered AI governance, responsible and participatory data systems, civic sense-making, system dynamics and agent-based modelling, with particular attention to the Global South and to people and communities often underrepresented in conventional data, technology, and policy processes.

Irwansyah is a lecturer and researcher in the Department of Communication, Faculty of Social and Political Sciences, Universitas Indonesia. His research focuses on digital communication, artificial intelligence, platform governance, responsible AI, and the social implications of emerging technologies. He is particularly interested in how AI systems, digital platforms, and algorithmic infrastructures shape communication, public participation, institutional practices, and inequalities in Global South contexts. His current work examines responsible AI, AI-mediated communication, digital governance, and the relationship between technological development and sustainable futures. Through interdisciplinary and comparative research, he seeks to contribute communication perspectives to evidence-based AI policy and governance, with particular attention to Indonesia and Southeast Asia.

I am a policy and innovation researcher interested in technological catch-up, technological innovation systems, and the economic impacts of artificial intelligence. My current research explores how AI reshapes labour markets, skill formation, and structural change, and how innovation policies can support inclusive and sustainable technological development.

Dr. John Oloo Gwendo is a Kenyan academic, researcher, and Information Technology specialist with expertise in artificial intelligence, knowledge-based systems, computing, and educational technology. He holds a PhD in Information Technology from Unicaf University and is a Lecturer at Moi University, where he teaches and supervises research in computing and information technology.
I am the head of PMO in cassava AI where I lead governance, control, change and research work. I have a long history of global AI governance advocacy within both impact and industry.

Kenneth Leonard is a GAFAI Delegate and Generative AI Engineer specializing in UN Responsible AI Governance, global leadership, and climate AI. With 25+ years bridging technology and sustainable development across Africa, he holds UN-certified credentials in Responsible AI (UNU-EHS), AI Governance & Equity (LinkedIn/UN partners), Disaster Risk Management (UNDRR), and Green Economy Leadership (UNITAR). His work ensures AI systems are ethically governed, climate-resilient, and accountable to the communities they serve.

Dr. Ali Bakeer is a Libyan academic, AI policy advisor, and digital transformation expert. He is an Associate Professor at Misurata University and Director of Research and Consultation Programs, leading digitalization and data-driven transformation initiatives. He serves as an Advisor to UNESCWA, contributing to the development of Libya’s National AI Strategy and Open Public Data Policy. His work focuses on responsible AI governance, data policy, digital transformation, and building institutional capacity for AI in libya.

Stéphanie is a legal officer at the Digital Governance Unit of Madagascar, which is a legal body structure attached to the Presidency of the Republic. She has studied about public law and Human rights. She is passionated about project management, digital transformation (including data Governance and AI) and public Policy. She has worked for three years and a half in a world-bank funded project about digital Governance and Identity Management System (PRODIGY).

Williams Stonard Kaphika is a Malawi-based interdisciplinary researcher and AI governance practitioner, with a background in physics, mathematics, and computational research. He is an AFRI-SPARC AI Policy & Research Fellow and the Founder & Research Lead at TPP RAIDA, where he focuses on AI governance, policy implementation, institutional capacity, and responsible AI in Africa. He leads the development of the Africa Responsible AI Policy Index (ARAPI), a comparative research initiative examining AI governance and implementation across African countries.

Lianna Adams is a Human-Centred AI Strategist, Digital Dignity Advocate, and Cognitive Culture Builder recognised by ForbesWeb3, Animoca Brands, and Open Campus as a 2024 Social Impact & Ethics leader and named one of the Top 10 Rising Women in Crypto 2023 including Best Women-led Startup to Watch 2025.

She has spoken at WEF, COP28, TEDx Youth, NFTNYC (four consecutive years), the World Web3.0 & AI Summit, EmpowHer AI, and Web3 Amsterdam, among others.

Her work centres on one urgent question: what do we preserve of ourselves as artificial intelligence transforms how we think, create, and relate? Through keynotes, workshops, and consulting, she helps organisations and communities build cultures where technology amplifies human capability without eroding cognitive autonomy, creative identity, or dignity.

She is the founder and creator of the Human-AI Cognitive Toolkit rooted in nine science-backed tools for cognitive wellness in an AI-saturated world and host of The Human Strata, a podcast and Substack essays exploring the human layer in the age of AI. She has hosted the Wirex Podcast and has convened 80,000+ community participants across digital events since 2021.

Lianna is also the founder of the Digital Dignity Initiative, leads the annual #16Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence campaign, and has served as a Non-Executive Director at Mental Health Spaces Collective.

She has been part of UNESCO's Women in Science working group, participated at UN Open Source Week and a member of AI2030, a community working on Responsible AI.

As Chair, I have steered the SIG's strategic direction under the defining theme of "Ethics and Governance in the Era of Ubiquitous AI." This was not an abstract intellectual exercise but a practical response to what I observed among information professionals globally. I was driven by a widespread uncertainty about engaging with AI systems ethically, a lack of institutional policy frameworks, and an urgent need for accessible governance tools. Under my leadership, SIG-IEP launched the Student Research Award on AI Governance, a $1,000 annual grant designed to fund student-led projects that advance transparent and responsible AI oversight. The inaugural award was won by Mary Anne Kochenderfer of San José State University, whose project,  "Generative AI for Libraries", is developing a publicly accessible platform to build AI governance literacy among library professionals.

members.biography:
Rooba Yanembal Moorghen is a senior public-policy and governance professional with more than four decades of experience in the Mauritius Civil Service, including service as Permanent Secretary and Accounting Officer across several ministries. Her career spans public administration, institutional governance, policy formulation, strategic planning, legislative development, public-sector accountability and international cooperation. She currently works as a freelance trainer in public policy and public administration.

As a former Permanent Secretary in the technology portfolio, she contributed to computerisation and e-government initiatives associated with the Digital Mauritius 2030 strategic plan. She also contributed to the drafting and finalisation of Mauritius’s Data Protection Act 2017 and participated in reviews of cybersecurity and cyber-related legislation, including work with the Council of Europe. From 2018 to 2020, she co-chaired the Advisory Board of the Global Forum on Cyber Expertise, supporting international dialogue and cyber-capacity cooperation.

Moorghen holds a PhD in Evaluation from the University of Birmingham. Her doctoral research examined the institutionalisation of evaluation in Mauritius and its role in evidence-informed policymaking, accountability and institutional learning. She has presented her findings to evaluation associations and at the University of Mauritius Research Week, where she received a Best Oral Speaker award. Her international engagement also includes the World Bank’s Women, Business and the Law work, the International Telecommunication Union and professional development in policy evaluation and behavioural science. She is undertaking further study in AI and Digital Transformation in Government through a course involving Saïd Business School, the University of Oxford and UNESCO.

As the Coalition’s International Research & Policy Lead, she will advance practical, evidence-based AI governance grounded in the realities of public institutions. Her committee focus on Public Policy & Institutional Implementation brings particular attention to government coordination, regulatory preparedness, data protection, transparency, accountability, workforce capacity and evaluation—especially in Small Island Developing States and other countries with varying administrative and digital resources.

For her first 90 days, she proposes a practitioner-oriented note provisionally titled “From AI Principles to Public-Sector Practice.” The work would examine what governments should consider before adopting AI in public services, including institutional readiness, data governance and legal safeguards, public accountability, workforce preparedness and evaluation of outcomes. She would invite country perspectives from Coalition members and develop a comparative learning framework to support responsible, context-sensitive implementation across the Global South.

For his doctoral candidacy, he secured the CAS-TWAS President’s Fellowship. He is currently a Research Mentor in the Directorate for Research Administration, Vice Presidency for Research, and a visiting faculty member in the different schools at Tecnologico de Monterrey, Mexico. He has been a member of the National System of Researchers (SNI) in Mexico’s Secretaría de Ciencia, Humanidades, Tecnología e Innovación (SECIHTI) since 2021. He has several publications in highly reputed journals and international conference proceedings and is part of editorial board, guest editor, and reviewer of many prestigious, indexed international journals and conferences. His current research focuses on public management and policy, technology and innovation management, and AI in education.

Jésica Tapia is an AI policy researcher, consultant, and AI developer with more than 15 years of experience spanning the public sector, academia, and applied AI. Her work sits at the intersection of AI policy and regulation, AI ethics and safety, and cooperative AI, with a sustained focus on gender and AI governance.

She is a member of CAIDP's AI Policy Group (Global Majority track) and of UNESCO's Women4Ethical AI leadership group, and a contributing author to CAIDP's Artificial Intelligence and Democratic Values Index. As CTO of Analítica Boutique, she designs and deploys applied AI systems — multi-agent architectures, RAG, NLP, and computer vision — and presented "Human-Centered AI Design and Inclusive Innovation" at an endorsed side event of the 2026 Global Dialogue on AI Governance.

She teaches at UNAM and UVM, coordinates and lectures in the Diploma in Data Science for the Social Sciences and Humanities at FES Acatlán–UNAM (seven cohorts since 2022), and co-founded IA para Mujeres, a program on the gender pay gap and women's leadership in generative AI.She is Claude Community Ambassador in México City for Social Sciences and Humanities.

My name is Robert O. Harmsen, originally from the Netherlands, but I have been working at Tecnologico de Monterrey, campus Queretaro, for the past 10 years. My background focuses in particular on International Relations and International Law, and I teach in both programmes at Tec. Furthermore, I have often been part of both design and coordination teams within the academic curricula at Tec (ranging from regular classes, electives up till entire semester-long specializations); as well as having held certain Director positions within my School (of Social Sciences and Government). Prof. Mohammed Khalil holds a PhD in Computer Science. He is a Full
Professor and researcher at Hassan II University of Casablanca at Faculty of Sciences and Technology of Mohammedia (FSTM).

Beyond his academic contributions, Prof. Khalil is a prominent advocate for the advancement of AI in Morocco. He is the co-founder and President of MoroccoAI, a leading non-profit organization dedicated to fostering excellence, collaboration, and innovation in the field of AI across the country.

From 2019 to 2021, he served as Director of Digital Transformation at Hassan II University, where he played a key role in shaping and implementing the institution's digital strategy. 

From 2021 to 2024, he joined the office of the Minister of Solidarity, Social Integration, and 
Family, where he led strategic initiatives to digitalize and modernize social services. From 
2022 to 2024, Prof. Khalil also worked as a digital transformation expert with the United 
Nations Development Programme (UNDP), contributing to national efforts to design and 
implement inclusive digital policies and solutions.

In 2025, he launched and co-chaired Morocco's inaugural AI Forum dedicated to AI  ethics, policy, and governance, in collaboration with META. In 2026, he partnered with GIZ to launch the second edition of the Women’s AI Forum, further advancing inclusive and  responsible AI.

I am a Deputy Director at Nepal Rastra Bank (Central Bank of Nepal), currently working in the Economic Analysis Division of the Economic Research Department. I have over 10 years of experience spanning macroeconomic research, financial regulation, public procurement, and strategic planning, having previously worked in Nepal Rastra Bank's regulatory and procurement departments, at Ncell (Nepal's largest telecom operator), and at Finastra and Wipro in India. I combine strong quantitative skills — R, SQL, Python, and Tableau — with deep expertise in financial systems, regulatory frameworks, and evidence-based policymaking, and have prepared research and reports for stakeholders including the IMF, World Bank, and Government of Nepal. I hold an MBA in Finance, a BSc in Computer Science, and am currently completing an MA in Economics at Tribhuvan University.

Dr Karaitiana Taiuru is a Māori AI, data, and emerging-technology ethicist who helps organisations understand how modern digital systems affect identity, rights, and equity outcomes. He delivers practical guidance for boards, agencies, and industry leaders on AI governance, Māori Data Sovereignty, IP, and preventing bias and discrimination across the AI lifecycle.

I have dual expertise in media and communication and artificial intelligence. I am a PhD holder in Mass Communication with professional experience as a broadcast journalist, and I am currently pursuing a Master’s degree in Artificial Intelligence. My interdisciplinary expertise enables me to explore the intersection of AI, media, communication, and society, combining practical media experience with advanced academic research and emerging technologies.

I'm an AI/ML researcher and Research Fellow at CPX Lab (CSU Long Beach), studying coordination failures and trust in multi-agent AI systems. My work spans a diagnostic framework for detecting adversarial and communication failures in multi-agent systems and an open-source tool for assessing AI compliance with the EU AI Act.
I came to AI research from a political science background, and I now focus on bridging technical AI development and governance, particularly accountability gaps in under-resourced regulatory contexts.

Imoh Ebenezer is the Founder of Datariom Core, a company dedicated to helping small and medium enterprises (SMEs) adopt Artificial Intelligence (AI) to drive growth, efficiency, and innovation. With a strong foundation in AI literacy, research commercialization, and technology-driven solutions, he operates at the intersection of innovation and real-world impact. 

Through Datariom Core, Imoh advances the belief that AI should not remain a distant concept for African businesses, but a practical tool for solving pressing challenges—from streamlining operations to unlocking new market opportunities. Central to this work is nForce, Datariom Core’s AI-powered platform for real-time fraud detection, risk monitoring, and automated AML compliance, designed specifically for financial institutions and agent-based networks. 

Through nForce, he is building systems that move organizations from reactive operations to proactive, intelligence-driven decision-making. 

Beyond Datariom Core, Imoh served as Chief Data Officer at the Grassroots Movement for Bola Ahmed Tinubu, where he leads data-driven strategy and analytics across Nigeria. He is also a contributor to the Nigeria Economic Summit Group (NESG), supporting the Policy Commission in advancing national conversations on technology, innovation, and economic transformation. 

At his core, Imoh sees Africa as a continent defined by creativity, resilience, and untapped potential. He believes the next wave of global innovation can emerge from Africa if young innovators are equipped with the right tools, mentorship, and access to technology. His vision is to position Africa not only as a participant in the global digital economy, but as a driver of it.

I am an AI governance and Responsible AI practitioner based in Nigeria, with a background in engineering. My work sits at the intersection of AI governance, Responsible AI, data protection, AI risk, ethics, and compliance.

I have experience contributing to AI governance frameworks, researching AI risks such as bias, and helping organizations understand how to use AI responsibly. I am particularly interested in how AI governance can be made practical and relevant to African and other Global South contexts.
I am Hassan Raji, an associate Product manager (AI focus), with background in Philosophy, I am presently look up masters in Data and information science. I am curious I love to seek clarity.

Malcolm Durosaye is an AI governance and technology strategy executive advancing responsible AI and digital transformation across Africa and the Global South. He is an AI Research Consultant at Dev-Afrique and Co-Founder of the Sandbox Hub at Net and Strategy Solution (https://sandbox.netandstrategy.com), where he leads initiatives at the intersection of technology, policy, and institutional capacity.

His work focuses on helping organizations navigate the strategic opportunities and risks of AI, from model evaluation and localization to technology risk management and responsible deployment. Malcolm is committed to strengthening African capacity to shape AI policy, governance, and standards, ensuring that Global South priorities are reflected in the technologies and institutions shaping the future.

I am the Founder and Executive Director of the Responsible AI Governance Initiative (RAI-GI), an independent public-interest nonprofit building the institutional capacity Africa needs to govern artificial intelligence safely, accountably, and in the public interest.

My work focuses on one of the defining governance challenges of our time: ensuring that governments, regulators, civil society, and industry possess the expertise, systems, and partnerships required to translate AI governance principles into effective institutional practice.

Through RAI-GI, I lead initiatives that strengthen AI governance through independent research, practical decision-maker training, multi-stakeholder partnerships, and implementation-focused policy support. Our work helps bridge the gap between AI governance ambition and institutional reality, enabling African institutions to adopt and govern advanced AI responsibly while protecting the public interest.

I believe Africa should not only participate in global conversations on AI governance but help shape them. The continent's experience, institutions, and perspectives are essential to building governance frameworks that are effective, inclusive, and globally relevant.

My long-term ambition is to contribute to building trusted institutions capable of governing increasingly powerful AI systems while positioning Africa as a leading voice in the future of global AI governance.

Nuraini Usman is a data scientist, academic, researcher, and technology professional from Nigeria with over seven years of experience spanning data science and analytics, information technology, data governance, internet governance, cybersecurity, and digital transformation. He holds a Master of Technology in Data Science and Analytics from Universiti Teknikal Malaysia Melaka and a Bachelor of Information Technology from the International University of East Africa. He currently serves as a Lecturer II in Computer Science at the Federal University of Technology, Babura, where he combines teaching, research, and institutional research and innovation activities. His research interests include responsible and explainable artificial intelligence, machine learning, data governance, digital inclusion, AI policy, and emerging technology governance. He also serves as a Regional Coordinator for the Internet Society Nigeria Chapter, supporting initiatives on internet governance, digital rights, data governance, and inclusive digital development. His research and publications have examined AI, machine learning, DNS policy, big data, digital security, and technology applications in healthcare.

Dr. Obasesam Okoi is an Associate Professor of Justice and Peace Studies at the University of St. Thomas in Minnesota and Founding Director of the AI & Society Innovation Lab. His work focuses on AI governance, AI policy, responsible AI, and AI ethics, particularly their implications for societies in Africa and the Global South. He is interested in how governance frameworks can ensure that artificial intelligence advances human dignity, social justice, inclusive development, and the public good while addressing emerging technological risks and inequalities. Through interdisciplinary research, teaching, policy engagement, and the AI & Society Innovation Lab, he contributes to conversations on building human-centered and socially responsible approaches to AI governance.

Olaolu Oluwasanmi’s research focuses on international migration, diaspora engagement, diaspora studies, and urban development, particularly in relation to state agency, belonging, and citizenship. Pretty Tega Edema, PhD, is an academic, legal researcher and AI ethics and governance professional working across law, artificial intelligence, data protection, digital rights and technology policy in Africa. She is a Lecturer at Admiralty University of Nigeria and Research Lead at the Pan Africa Centre for AI Ethics, where she studies the ethical, legal and societal implications of AI and emerging technologies.

She is Education and Training Director of the Data Privacy Lawyers Association of Nigeria, designing practical training for lawyers and other professionals working in data protection, privacy and technology law. She founded the Privacy, Online Safety and Technology Hub to strengthen digital-rights awareness and online-safety education among young people and students. Her professional fellowships include the Policy and Innovation Center, the West Africa School of Internet Governance and the Africa Privacy Book Club.

Edema has authored four books on data privacy and protection: Artificial Intelligence in African Context: An Overview of Key Issues; A Glossary of Data Privacy and Data Protection; Forms and Precedents in Data Privacy Law; and Compendium of Nigerian Data Privacy Protection Laws. Her peer-reviewed research addresses image rights, privacy regulation, judicial approaches to data protection, AI ethics and emerging technology law. She also participated in the West Africa Internet Governance Forum 2026 panels on child online protection, online trust, platform accountability and human capacity development.

As Chair and Strategic Coordination Lead of the Coalition, she aims to establish clear priorities, coordinate collaborative research and turn shared objectives into measurable outcomes. Her existing committee focus is AI Governance, Law & Rights, including African AI regulation, legal accountability, data protection, digital rights and youth online safety. She emphasizes focused cross-regional collaboration and practical research grounded in Global South legal and institutional contexts.

For her first 90 days, she proposes a comparative working paper on AI liability and accountability in public decision-making across selected Global South countries. Rather than a broad survey, the work would examine concrete cases, assess legal responsibility and institutional accountability, identify gaps in safeguards and consider transparency, rights and ways to challenge AI-assisted decisions. The proposed output would provide practical policy recommendations and a foundation for further Coalition research.

Jannatul Nayem is a graduate student in International Relations at Jahangirnagar University, Bangladesh. Her research interests include AI governance, responsible AI, digital rights, and public policy. She has contributed to international AI research initiatives through MLCommons and Cohere Labs, focusing on AI benchmarking and systemic risk governance. She has also completed several AI-related courses, including Developing AI Policy, Ethical and Regulatory Implications of Generative AI, and Responsible Generative AI, and participated in international summer schools on AI safety, climate change AI, and ENAIS.

I am a graduate in Banking and Insurance from the University of Chittagong, with a growing focus on AI safety and governance as one of the most consequential challenges facing civic society and institutions today. Since July 2026, I have been a founding member of AI Safety Bangladesh, a budding community working to build awareness of advanced AI risks, governance, and data protection among people across Bangladesh. In this role, I contribute to organizational structure-building, outreach, and research aimed at educating the public on the long-term consequences of advanced AI, including risks associated with AGI.

My academic training in banking, finance, and organizational behavior, combined with leadership experience gained through student and community organizations at the University of Chittagong, has given me a practical understanding of institutional structures, governance, and coordinated decision-making. I bring this perspective to AI safety work, believing that protecting society from the risks of advanced AI requires not only technical understanding but also strong institutions, informed civic engagement, and cross-border cooperation.

Sohan Bapary is an AI-Legal Architect and Computational Law Researcher (LL.M.) specialising in cross-border digital sovereignty, algorithmic accountability, and automated compliance. He bridges the gap between international legal doctrine and systems architecture by engineering "policy-as-code." He is the creator of Vigilanci and IGRIS Core—platforms designed to align autonomous software workflows with international regulatory standards (GDPR, EU AI Act). He currently manages data protection operations at Datawallet while advancing academic research on autonomous agent liability.

I am Tustee Mazumdar, currently an AI Safety Research Fellow at the PRISM AI Safety Research Fellowship, an initiative by Women Who Do Data (W2D2), where I work on Trust Calibration in Healthcare AI.  I graduated with a B.Sc. in Computer Science from Asian University for Women. 
I aspire to build robust, trustworthy, and inclusive AI systems that are reliable in high-stakes settings and accessible to underrepresented languages and communities.

Oscar Cariceo Rivera is a Software Engineer, Anthropologist, and Master of Social Work with over 12 years of experience bridging technical AI development, regulatory compliance, and human-centered design in the Global South. As the Founder of KintuAI, he builds applied Explainable AI (XAI) solutions and governance frameworks that make algorithmic decisions auditable, transparent, and fair. Concurrently, as UX Research Manager at Scotiabank Chile, he leads cross-functional teams to evaluate and mitigate the human, operational, and adoption risks of automated systems in highly regulated financial environments. A selected Fellow of the BID fAIr-LAC initiative, Oscar specializes in translating abstract AI governance principles into practical, operational controls, ensuring that AI deployment in Latin America is equitable, traceable, and aligned with both local regulatory mandates and global responsible AI standards.

Dr. S. Poornima is an accomplished academician and researcher in Computer Science and Engineering with over 19 years of teaching, research, and academic leadership experience. She currently serves as Associate Professor at S-VYASA University, Bengaluru, specializing in Deep Learning, Artificial Intelligence, Cyber Security, and Machine Learning. She earned her Ph.D. in Deep Learning/AI from Presidency University, Bengaluru (2024) and has successfully led funded research projects, published extensively in reputed Scopus-indexed journals and conferences, and contributed to several patents in AI and intelligent systems. Dr. S. Poornima has organized numerous national and international academic events, mentored student innovation initiatives, and serves as a reviewer for international journals. Her research interests include AI-driven healthcare, malware detection, IoT security, explainable AI, and intelligent decision-support systems. She is recognized with several awards, including the AICTE Innovation Ambassador Award (2025) and Best Faculty Awards, reflecting her commitment to excellence in teaching, research, and innovation.

Oluwaseyi is a sustainable development expert working on migration governance and environment.

Sharon Juwah is an AI governance specialist who centres her work on a fundamental question: when an AI system acts inside an institution, who is held liable, and is there a capacity to assess? 
Her work focuses on agentic AI liability, AI incident reporting, and the institutional and technical capacity regulators need to independently assess AI systems and enforce governance requirements.
She applies this work in practice as Head of AI Innovation at Afari Travels & Tours, where she leads the organisation's responsible AI initiatives and contributes to research and the development of governance processes for AI-enabled operations.
She is also the Convener of On the Books, a web series examining AI governance across Africa, and speaks on AI governance and policy at international forums.
Her research on strategic AI sovereignty examines how African states can exercise meaningful control over critical AI dependencies and develop the capacity to independently verify the systems deployed within their jurisdictions.

Dr. Victor Moinina is a Sierra Leonean governance scholar, policy strategist and regional integration expert with more than a decade of experience in peacebuilding, institutional development and youth and gender empowerment across Africa.

He holds a PhD in Governance and Regional Integration (with Distinction) and an MSc in the same field from the Pan African University Institute for Governance, Humanities and Social Sciences, University of Yaoundé II, Cameroon. His first degree is a BA from Fourah Bay College, University of Sierra Leone.

His career began in peacebuilding as National Early Warning Systems Manager at WANEP-Sierra Leone, followed by a role as Programme Policy Officer with the World Food Programme in Ethiopia’s Somali Region, where he served as an African Union Youth Volunteer. Today he is Assistant Head of Department (Leadership and Development) and Lecturer at the Institute of Public Administration and Management (IPAM), University of Sierra Leone. He is also Executive Director and Lead Consultant of Pro-Idealist Limited, the research and consultancy firm he founded in 2021.

He chairs the board of Advocate for the Rights of Women and Girls Sierra Leone and serves as Policy and Research Lead at VIONet Sierra Leone. He has published peer-reviewed research on the green economy, energy security and civil society, and has supported a national civil society assessment of Sierra Leone’s progress on the SDGs.

His recognitions include the Pan African Youth Development Activist of the Year award and selection as Global Youth Ambassador for Sierra Leone. He is also an alumnus of the Mo Ibrahim Foundation Residential School on Governance and Development and the Young African Leaders Initiative (YALI), and has presented youth employment and Agenda 2063 outcomes to the African Union Commission.

I am an Associate Professor of Information Systems at the University of Dodoma, Tanzania. My research looks at how AI and digital technologies are adopted and governed in public services, businesses, agriculture, and education. Recent work covers AI agents and data protection requirements, generative AI use in software development, mobile AI services in Tanzanian manufacturing firms, and a comparison of data protection laws across East African countries. I also work on electronic government and its link to the Sustainable Development Goals. I serve as an academic editor at PLOS ONE and review for several information systems journals. I teach and supervise postgraduate students.

I am a PhD researcher at the University of Cambridge, working on political thought and transregional connections between Iran and East Asia. My broader interests lie in technology, public policy and the Global South. Alongside my academic research, I have worked in policy and consulting roles, including research on smart cities and digital infrastructure across the Middle East and North Africa and sustainable development work with UNESCO-ICUA. I am particularly interested in how emerging AI technologies interact with different political, social and institutional contexts across Asia and the wider Global South.

I am an educator with over 25 years of experience. My focus is on bringing community and classroom together to empower students to use academic, 21st-century, and 3rd-millennium skills to learn about and improve issues that impact their communities.

Gina Grant, M.Ed., is Founder and CEO of CoreKind, a human-centered innovation studio focused on responsible AI and the future of learning and work. With more than 20 years of experience across education, workforce development, and social innovation, she has helped institutions build the capacity to adopt emerging technologies in ways that center human dignity, strengthen agency, and expand equitable access to opportunity.
Her work bridges human-centered design, responsible technology, and institutional transformation, with a particular focus on ensuring that the people and communities most affected by technological change have a meaningful voice in shaping it. Her experience spans education, community-based innovation, and workforce development, including digital literacy initiatives for justice-impacted learners.
In November 2026, she will participate as a panelist at the Africa Celebrates Women Forum in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, contributing to conversations on women's leadership, innovation, and the future of African and global communities.

Marty brings invaluable cross border governance & multi disciplinary fiduciary expertise that will strengthen RAI-GI's mission to advance responsible AI governance, digital rights, and trusted data stewardship across Africa and beyond. This appointment marks an important milestone as we continue building a globally connected faceted stakeholder coalition dedicated to ensuring that AI serves humanity responsibly.

Wafa Al-Daily is an international executive leader, urban planner and policy strategist with more than 25 years of experience across governments, multilateral organisations, academia and international development. Her work spans institutional governance, strategic planning, urban development, education, inclusive development and post-conflict recovery, with particular engagement in developing countries, the Middle East and North Africa, and fragile and conflict-affected settings.

She is Co-Founder and Executive Director of EHAAR International and Vice President for Governance, Strategy and Policy at the International Society of City and Regional Planners (ISOCARP). Her leadership includes institutional strategy, international partnerships and coordination of multi-stakeholder initiatives. She holds a PhD in Planning, Governance and Globalization from Virginia Tech.

Her international development work has included collaboration with the World Bank, Virginia Tech, governments and development partners on institutional reform, urban inclusion, universal accessibility, education and capacity-building. Under the SERATAC II initiative, she managed a STEM education assessment in Palestine drawing on 64 classroom observations across six education directorates. She has also engaged in policy dialogue on AI, digital cooperation and data privacy, and on the implications of emerging technologies for cities and vulnerable communities.

As Chair and Strategic Coordination Lead of the Coalition, Al-Daily prioritises credible governance, transparent decision-making, clear responsibilities, research independence and measurable outcomes. Her AI-governance perspective centres on public accountability, regulatory capacity, digital inclusion, human rights and data sovereignty, while recognising that policy must fit different institutional resources, structures and levels of public trust.

For her first 90 days, she proposes a Coalition Strategic Priorities and Coordination Framework developed through structured consultation with the founding committee and Atlas AI Institute. It would assess institutional needs and member expertise, identify three research and policy priorities, define leadership responsibilities and decision-making, and set out a proposed 12-month roadmap. Her proposed milestones are a consultation draft by Day 45, committee review by Day 60, and a final framework with a documented decision and action log by Day 90.

I am a graduate student in Cybersecurity at New York University with a background in computer science and community-facing technology work. For four years, I have served as a frontline technology support specialist in a public library system, where I directly supported thousands of diverse users navigating digital systems, which taught me how technology inclusion varies dramatically based on institutional and resource constraints.

My research has focused on systemic vulnerabilities with global implications: international cybercrime enforcement gaps, privacy vulnerabilities in operating systems, and emerging AI-generated threats. This work is grounded in the conviction that technology safety and security cannot be achieved in isolation, but requires understanding how vulnerabilities and solutions affect different communities differently, particularly those with fewer resources and institutional safeguards.

I hold a Teaching Certification in Computer Science and have mentored students and community members on digital literacy and technology access. I am currently pursuing my Master's degree while maintaining my library work, blending academic research with direct community engagement.
